## 1\. Introduction and System Overview

This report documents the design, implementation, and security architecture of our CSE447 Lab Project: **BiteRush 2.0**. Our system is a full-stack food ordering and culinary community web application designed around defense-in-depth security principles.

In standard commercial web applications, developers frequently rely on high-level database drivers or built-in framework helpers to handle security. In this project, to rigorously explore low-level mathematical security, **all core cryptographic algorithms—including RSA encryption, Elliptic Curve (ECC) ElGamal encryption, SHA-256 hashing, HMAC data integrity, and One-Time Password (OTP) derivation—were built completely from scratch** using JavaScript/TypeScript BigInt primitives without relying on third-party cryptography libraries.

---

### 1.1 Project Overview

BiteRush 2.0 is an online food delivery platform and community hub built to serve four everyday user groups:

1. **Customers**: Browse restaurant menus, place multi-item orders across flexible delivery tiers (Saver, Standard, Priority), track order progress in real-time, communicate directly with their assigned delivery rider, and share reviews and food stories on a community board.  
2. **Restaurant Managers**: Supervise live kitchen operations, manage menu availability, accept incoming customer orders, and dispatch available delivery riders.  
3. **Delivery Riders**: Access a dedicated deliveries queue, view drop-off coordinates and delivery instructions, chat with customers for route clarifications, and mark orders delivered.  
4. **Administrators**: Inspect platform accounts, oversee global orders, monitor system security health, and manage cryptographic keys (including key distribution and on-demand key rotation).

The central security mission of BiteRush 2.0 is **database compromise resistance**: even if an adversary gains direct, unauthorized access to the underlying MongoDB database (via SQL/NoSQL injection or stolen database dumps), they cannot read customer names, email addresses, phone numbers, delivery coordinates, rider chats, or community posts. All sensitive attributes are encrypted before writing to disk and decrypted only in server memory for authenticated users.

---

### 1.2 Technology Stack

Our system is built using modern web technologies paired with a standalone, custom-built cryptography engine:

* **Frontend & UI Layer**:  
  * [Next.js 15](https://nextjs.org/) (App Router architecture with React 19\)  
  * [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/) and [Radix UI](https://www.radix-ui.com/) accessible components  
  * [Lucide Icons](https://lucide.dev/) for intuitive visual status indicators  
* **Backend Runtime**:  
  * Node.js (v18+) with strict TypeScript for type safety across API boundaries  
  * Next.js Server Components and RESTful Route Handlers  
* **Database & Persistence**:  
  * [MongoDB](https://www.mongodb.com/) NoSQL database managed via [Mongoose 8 ODM](https://mongoosejs.com/)  
* **Authentication Framework**:  
  * [NextAuth.js v4](https://next-auth.js.org/) using a custom stateless JWT strategy and role claims  
* **Password Hashing**:  
  * bcryptjs (configured with 10 salt rounds for secure password derivation)  
* **Email Service**:  
  * nodemailer (for delivering out-of-band 2FA verification codes)  
* **Custom Cryptography Subsystem (src/lib/crypto/)**:  
  * **No external crypto libraries or built-in framework helpers were used.**  
  * math.ts: Arbitrary-precision BigInt arithmetic, modular exponentiation (modPow), modular inverse (modInverse), Miller-Rabin primality testing, and the Tonelli-Shanks algorithm.  
  * sha256.ts: Complete SHA-256 implementation adhering to RFC 6234\.  
  * hmac.ts: RFC 2104 compliant HMAC-SHA256 message authentication and deterministic blind lookup tokens.  
  * rsa.ts: 1024-bit RSA key generation, PKCS\#1 v1.5 random padding, and modular exponentiation chunking.  
  * ecc.ts: secp256k1 elliptic curve arithmetic, point addition, point doubling, Koblitz message embedding, and ElGamal asymmetric encryption.  
  * otp.ts: RFC 4226 dynamic truncation for two-factor authentication code generation.  
  * keyManager.ts: Multi-version key storage and rotation coordinator.

## 2\. Login and Registration Module

User registration and login are foundational to application security. We structured both flows to protect sensitive information during transit, while stored at rest, and throughout active sessions.

#### Step-by-Step Registration Security Pipeline

| Step \# | Pipeline Stage | Cryptographic Primitive | Implementation Details & Purpose |
| :---: | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1** | Input Normalization | String Sanitization | Extra spaces trimmed; email converted to lowercase to prevent casing mismatches. |
| **2** | Password Hashing | bcrypt (10 rounds) | Generates unique 128-bit salt per user; slow hash derivation makes offline cracking infeasible. |
| **3** | Blind Indexing | HMAC-SHA256 (Server Pepper) | Computes deterministic blind tokens for email and phone without exposing plaintext in database. |
| **4** | Uniqueness Check | MongoDB Query | Checks if blind tokens already exist. If found, aborts with 409 Conflict. |
| **5** | Asymmetric Encryption | RSA-1024 (PKCS\#1 v1.5) | Encrypts firstName, lastName, email, contactNumber, and addresses into versioned envelopes. |
| **6** | Data Integrity MAC | HMAC-SHA256 | Calculates integrityMac over the canonical string of all encrypted fields to prevent tampering. |
| **7** | Database Persistence | Mongoose ODM / MongoDB | Persists ciphertext envelopes; standard plaintext fields are overwritten with "\[ENCRYPTED\]". |
| **8** | 2FA Code Generation | OTP Dynamic Truncation | Generates 6-digit email verification OTP valid for 10 minutes; dispatches via SMTP. |

#### Authentication Protocol Breakdown

| Phase | Action | Endpoint / Component | Security Rule & Verification Logic |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Phase 1: Step 1** | User Identification | /api/auth/login-challenge | User supplies identifier and raw password. Server computes blind HMAC to fetch user without plaintext query. |
| **Phase 1: Step 2** | Password Validation | bcrypt.compare | Compares raw password against salted Blowfish hash in constant time. Rejects invalid credentials with 401\. |
| **Phase 1: Step 3** | OTP Challenge Issue | CryptoService.generateOTP | Derives 6-digit code using HMAC dynamic truncation. Saves in DB with 10-minute expiry; emails user. |
| **Phase 2: Step 4** | OTP Challenge Submit | NextAuth CredentialsProvider | User supplies credentials \+ 6-digit code. Provider invokes CryptoService.verifyOTP checking code and expiry. |
| **Phase 2: Step 5** | Anti-Replay & Decrypt | Server Memory (RAM) | Single-use: OTP immediately wiped from database. User's RSA encrypted name is decrypted in RAM only. |
| **Phase 2: Step 6** | Session Establishment | NextAuth JWT Cookie | Mints HMAC-signed JWT in HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie containing role claims. |

### 2.3 Implementation Details Table

| Requirement | Implementation in BiteRush 2.0 |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Login Module** | Implemented in src/app/api/auth/login-challenge/route.ts and src/app/api/auth/\[...nextauth\]/option.ts. Enforces primary password authentication, followed by a mandatory 6-digit OTP verification before issuing a session. |
| **Registration Module** | Implemented in src/app/api/sign-up/route.ts. Collects user credentials, validates uniqueness via blind HMAC tokens, encrypts PII, computes an integrity tag, and stores the user record. |
| **Data Encrypted Before Storage** | User PII fields (firstName, lastName, email, contactNumber, bio, restaurantAddress, vehicleType) are encrypted with **from-scratch RSA-1024**; community posts and order addresses are encrypted with **from-scratch ECC secp256k1 ElGamal**. |
| **Data Decrypted on Retrieval** | During profile viewing (/api/user/profile) or session initialization, the system reads ciphertext envelopes, verifies data integrity, and decrypts the plaintext using the server's private key. |

A core project requirement is that **symmetric encryption (such as AES or DES) is strictly disallowed**, and that the system must implement **at least two different asymmetric algorithms** for separate parts of the application.

### 3.2 Encryption Algorithm — RSA Implementation

Our RSA engine is implemented from scratch in `src/lib/crypto/rsa.ts`, supported by BigInt number theory functions in `src/lib/crypto/math.ts`:

1. **Key Generation**:  
   * The engine generates two distinct 512-bit probable prime numbers, $p$ and $q$, using a custom Miller-Rabin primality test running 40 independent rounds ($k = 40$).  
   * Modulus: $n = p \times q$ (yielding a 1024-bit modulus).  
   * Euler's totient is calculated as: $\phi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1)$.  
   * The public exponent is set to the standard Fermat prime: $e = 65537$.  
   * The private exponent $d$ is derived as the modular multiplicative inverse:  
     $$d \equiv e^{-1} \pmod{\phi(n)}$$

2. **Modular Exponentiation & Block Chunking**:  
   * Long strings are segmented into chunks of at most 117 bytes ($128 - 11$ bytes reserved for PKCS#1 v1.5 padding).  
   * Encryption: $c \equiv m^e \pmod{n}$  
   * Decryption: $m \equiv c^d \pmod{n}$  
   * Computed via the binary square-and-multiply algorithm (`modPow`).

---

### 3.3 Encryption Algorithm — ECC Implementation

Our Elliptic Curve Cryptography engine is implemented from scratch in `src/lib/crypto/ecc.ts` using the standard **secp256k1** curve:

1. **Curve Parameters**:  
   * **Curve Equation (Short Weierstrass Form)**:  
     $$y^2 \equiv x^3 + ax + b \pmod{p}$$  
     where $a = 0$ and $b = 7$ for secp256k1:  
     $$y^2 \equiv x^3 + 7 \pmod{p}$$  
   * **Prime Field**:  
     $$p = 2^{256} - 2^{32} - 977$$

2. **Point Arithmetic**:  
   * **Point Addition**:  
     Given two points $P = (x_1, y_1)$ and $Q = (x_2, y_2)$ on the curve:  
     1. Distinct points ($P \neq Q$):  
        $$m \equiv \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \pmod{p}$$  
     2. Point doubling ($P = Q$):  
        $$m \equiv \frac{3x_1^2 + a}{2y_1} \pmod{p} = \frac{3x_1^2}{2y_1} \pmod{p}$$  
     3. Resulting point $R = P + Q = (x_r, y_r)$:  
        $$x_r \equiv m^2 - x_1 - x_2 \pmod{p}$$  
        $$y_r \equiv m(x_1 - x_r) - y_1 \pmod{p}$$  
   * **Scalar Multiplication**:  
     Scalar multiplication is the repeated addition of a point:  
     $$kP = P + P + \dots + P \quad (k \text{ times})$$  
     Efficient computation uses the double-and-add method, analogous to binary modular exponentiation.

---

### 3.4 How Both Algorithms Are Used Differently

Rather than using a single algorithm uniformly across the platform, our architecture cleanly separates responsibilities:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
│                   CRYPTOGRAPHIC ASYMMETRIC DOMAINS                       │  
├─────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┤  
│         RSA-1024 DOMAIN             │       ECC SECP256K1 DOMAIN         │  
│   (Static Identity & Profile PII)   │ (Dynamic Activity & Transactions)  │  
├─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤  
│ • First Name & Last Name            │ • Community Post Titles & Content  │  
│ • Customer Email & Phone Number     │ • Order Shipping Addresses         │  
│ • User Profile Bio                  │ • Delivery Rider Special Notes     │  
│ • Restaurant Facility Address       │ • Live Customer-Rider Chat Messages│  
│ • Rider Vehicle Details             │ • Post-Delivery Customer Reviews   │  
├─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤  
│ Rationale: Established PKCS\#1 v1.5  │ Rationale: Shorter 256-bit keys,   │  
│ standards guarantee robust, stable  │ faster point math, and compact     │  
│ encryption for stationary account   │ ciphertext envelopes ideal for     │  
│ profile records.                    │ high-frequency operational writes. │  
└─────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘

This strict segregation guarantees that no single asymmetric algorithm handles all operations, satisfying the course requirements.

---

## 4\. Password Hashing and Salting

Passwords represent the primary credential for account authentication. They are never stored in plaintext and are protected against dictionary, rainbow table, and brute-force attacks.

---

### 4.1 Hashing Algorithm Used

The application uses the **bcrypt** password hashing algorithm (via bcryptjs with a work factor of 10 rounds).

**Design Justification:** Standard hash functions (such as bare SHA-256 or MD5) are designed for raw throughput, enabling modern GPUs to compute billions of hashes per second. If an attacker dumps a database of standard SHA-256 password hashes, offline dictionary attacks can quickly recover common passwords. In contrast, bcrypt uses an expensive key setup derived from the Blowfish cipher. It is intentionally slow, memory-intensive, and computationally demanding, making mass offline cracking economically and technically infeasible.

---

### 4.2 Salt Generation

For every user account created, bcrypt automatically generates a cryptographically secure 128-bit (16-byte) random salt.

The resulting salt is stored directly within the modular string representation inside the passwordHash field:

$2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy  
├──┘├──┘└──────────────────────┘└────────────────────────────┘  
alg cost   128-bit Salt (22 chars)    184-bit Hash (31 chars)

Because the salt is uniquely generated per user, two users with identical passwords will always produce completely different hash strings, neutralizing rainbow-table attacks.

---

### 4.3 Verification Process

During authentication in src/app/api/auth/login-challenge/route.ts and src/app/api/auth/\[...nextauth\]/option.ts:

1. The user supplies their candidate password.  
2. The server reads the existing passwordHash string from the user's database record.  
3. The server invokes bcrypt.compare(candidatePassword, storedHash).  
4. The function extracts the salt and work factor from the stored string, applies the algorithm to the candidate password, and performs a constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks.

---

## 5\. Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)

To ensure access cannot be gained through stolen or leaked passwords alone, BiteRush 2.0 enforces two-step authentication for all accounts.

---

### 5.1 2FA Method

* **Second Factor Type**: Out-of-band, time-bounded One-Time Password (OTP) dispatched via email or presented through an interactive challenge interface.  
* **Underlying Algorithm**: Built from scratch in src/lib/crypto/otp.ts. The engine uses HMAC-SHA256 with a shared secret and a time/random counter, deriving a 6-digit numeric code via **RFC 4226 dynamic truncation**.  
* **Lifecycle Rules**:  
  * Valid for exactly 10 minutes (twoFactorOtpExpiresAt).  
  * Upon successful verification, the code is immediately wiped from the database record (twoFactorOtp \= undefined) to prevent replay attacks.  
  * Sessions are only minted if both the password and the OTP validate successfully.

---

### 5.2 Code Snippet

The following excerpt from our NextAuth authorization pipeline (src/app/api/auth/\[...nextauth\]/option.ts) shows how the two factors are validated before creating the user's session:

*// Validate primary credentials first*  
const isPasswordCorrect \= await bcrypt.compare(rawPassword, user.passwordHash);

if (isPasswordCorrect) {  
  *// Step 2: Validate the second factor (OTP)*  
  const isOtpValid \= CryptoService.verifyOTP(  
    inputOtp,  
    user.twoFactorOtp,  
    user.twoFactorOtpExpiresAt  
  );

  if (\!isOtpValid) {  
    return null; *// Reject session: missing, invalid, or expired OTP*  
  }

  *// Clear the OTP immediately to prevent replay attacks*  
  user.twoFactorOtp \= undefined;  
  user.twoFactorOtpExpiresAt \= undefined;  
  user.isTwoFactorVerified \= true;  
  await user.save();

  *// Decrypt RSA-encrypted profile fields to populate the active session*  
  const decryptedFirstName \= user.firstNameEncrypted  
    ? CryptoService.decryptProfile(user.firstNameEncrypted)  
    : user.firstName;  
      
  return { id: user.\_id.toString(), firstName: decryptedFirstName, role: user.role };  
}

---

## 6\. Key Management Module

The platform includes a dedicated Key Management Module to control key lifecycles, distribution, and rotation.

---

### 6.1 Key Storage Security

Implemented in src/lib/crypto/keyManager.ts:

* **In-Memory Keystore**: Active private keys are maintained in memory in an indexed KeyRing map (Map\<number, KeyRing\>).  
* **Environment Isolation**: In production, master keys can be provided via environment variables (CRYPTO\_RSA\_PRIVATE\_KEY, CRYPTO\_ECC\_PRIVATE\_KEY, and CRYPTO\_PEPPER\_SECRET), keeping sensitive private exponents off the filesystem.  
* **Safe Public Distribution**: Administrators can inspect public key material and cryptographic algorithms via `GET /api/admin/keys`. The private components ($d$ exponent and private scalar) are strictly held in memory and are never returned.

---

### 6.2 Key Rotation Policy

A major challenge in encrypted databases is rotating keys without invalidating historical data or requiring costly offline database migrations.

![][image5]

**Figure 6.1:** *Zero-downtime key rotation and multi-version KeyRing lifecycle.*

#### Monospace Key Lifecycle & Rotation Architecture

┌─────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────┐  
│ 1\. Admin Triggers       │ ────▶ │ 2\. Key Generation       │ ────▶ │ 3\. KeyRing Registration │  
│ POST /api/admin/keys    │       │ Generate new RSA-1024   │       │ Store new version into  │  
│ Increment version (v+1) │       │ and ECC secp256k1 pairs │       │ in-memory Map registry  │  
└─────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────┘       └────────────┬────────────┘  
                                                                                 │  
                                     ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┐  
                                     │                                                                                       │  
                                     ▼                                                                                       ▼  
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐  
                    │ Branch A: Future Writes         │                                     │ Branch B: Historical Reads      │  
                    │ • Encrypt with active version   │                                     │ • Read envelope "v" attribute   │  
                    │ • Envelope: {"v": 2, ...}       │                                     │ • Lookup historical key in Map  │  
                    │ • Zero DB downtime              │                                     │ • 100% backward compatible      │  
                    └─────────────────────────────────┘                                     └─────────────────────────────────┘

#### Key Lifecycle & Rotation Strategy

| Stage | Operation | Component | Security & Availability Rule |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. Trigger** | Admin Endpoint Call | /api/admin/keys (POST) | Restricted strictly to the admin role via Next.js edge middleware. Increments active key version  |
| **2\. Keygen** | Fresh Keypair Creation | RSA.generateKeyPair(), ECC.generateKeyPair() | Computes brand-new 1024-bit RSA modulus/exponents and 256-bit ECC scalar/point pairs completely in server RAM using BigInt. |
| **3\. Registration** | KeyRing Map Storage | KeyManager.keyRings (Map\<number, KeyRing\>) | Registers the new keys under the new version index. Historical keyrings remain intact in memory. |
| **4\. Future Writes** | Forward Encryption | CryptoService.encryptProfile(), encryptData() | All future database inserts embed the new version number in the envelope Requires zero database table locks. |
| **5\. Past Reads** | Backward Decryption | CryptoService.decryptProfile(), decryptData() | Decryptor inspects envelope version tag (v), dynamically fetches that version's private key from the KeyRing, ensuring complete backward compatibility. |

flowchart TD  
    Admin\["1. Admin POST /api/admin/keys"\] \--\> Bump\["2. Increment Version (v \= v \+ 1)"\]  
    Bump \--\> Gen\["3. Generate Fresh RSA-1024 & ECC Keypairs"\]  
    Gen \--\> Register\["4. Store in In-Memory KeyRing Registry"\]  
    Register \--\> Writes\["Future Writes: Encrypt using New Key (v=2)"\]  
    Register \--\> Reads\["Historical Reads: Decrypt using Stored Key (v=1)"\]

## 7\. Post and Profile Management

Users can create, view, and edit community posts, as well as view and update their profiles. Both modules encrypt data before storage and decrypt it on retrieval.

---

### 7.1 Post Module

Community posts allow customers to publish food reviews, share recipes, and recommend restaurants.

* **Create Flow** (POST /api/posts):  
  1. The user enters a title, content, and category on the community page (/community).  
  2. The server encrypts both title and content using **ECC secp256k1 ElGamal**.  
  3. The server computes an HMAC-SHA256 integrity tag over the encrypted fields.  
  4. The record is written with "\[ENCRYPTED\]" in plaintext fields and the ciphertext in titleEncrypted and contentEncrypted.  
* **Read Flow** (GET /api/posts):  
  1. The server queries the posts collection.  
  2. The server verifies the HMAC integrity tag for each post.  
  3. The server decrypts titleEncrypted and contentEncrypted using the ECC private key.  
  4. The decrypted posts are returned to the client with an active verification badge.  
* **Update Flow** (PUT /api/posts/\[id\]):  
  1. The server confirms the requester is either the original author or an administrator.  
  2. Revisions are re-encrypted with ECC ElGamal, the HMAC tag is recalculated, and the document is updated.

---

### 7.2 Profile Module

Implemented in /api/user/profile and /api/user/update:

* **Profile View**: When a user navigates to /profile, the server verifies the record's integrity MAC, reads the RSA ciphertext fields (firstNameEncrypted, lastNameEncrypted, emailEncrypted, contactNumberEncrypted, bioEncrypted), decrypts them in memory, and displays them on the dashboard.  
* **Profile Update**: When updating details, the server re-encrypts updated attributes using the active RSA public key, re-indexes blind HMAC tokens, recomputes the user's integrityMac, and updates MongoDB.

---

## 9\. Message Authentication Code (MAC)

Encryption provides confidentiality, but does not inherently guarantee data integrity. If an adversary modifies database records directly, standard decryption might yield corrupted or manipulated information. We use Message Authentication Codes (MACs) to detect unauthorized changes.

---

### 9.1 MAC Algorithm Used

We implemented **HMAC-SHA256** completely from scratch in src/lib/crypto/hmac.ts:

* **Algorithm Selection Justification**:  
  1. We selected HMAC over CBC-MAC because CBC-MAC can be vulnerable to length-extension attacks when handling variable-length data, unless complex padding rules are enforced.  
  2. HMAC uses a standardized two-pass hashing structure that is mathematically secure against length-extension and collision vulnerabilities.  
* **From-Scratch Implementation**:  
  1. Key Normalization: The secret key is normalized to the 64-byte SHA-256 block size ($K'$).  
  2. Inner and Outer Padding:  
     $$\text{ipad} = K' \oplus 0x36^{64}$$  
     $$\text{opad} = K' \oplus 0x5C^{64}$$  
  3. Two-Pass Hash Calculation:  
     $$\text{HMAC}(K, m) = \text{SHA256}\Big(\text{opad} \parallel \text{SHA256}(\text{ipad} \parallel m)\Big)$$

---

### 9.2 Integrity Verification Flow

Integrity verification occurs automatically whenever encrypted records are accessed, ensuring zero compromised or tampered data is ever decrypted.

![][image6]

**Figure 9.1:** *HMAC-SHA256 tamper detection and data integrity verification flow.*

Monospace Tamper Detection & Integrity Flow

┌──────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐  
│ 1\. Read Request      │ ──────▶ │ 2\. Canonical Payload │ ──────▶ │ 3\. Calculate HMAC    │  
│ Client fetches post, │         │ Reconstruct string   │         │ Compute HMAC-SHA256  │  
│ profile, or order    │         │ from ciphertext data │         │ using server pepper  │  
└──────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘         └──────────┬───────────┘  
                                                                             │  
                                                                             ▼  
                                                                 ┌───────────────────────┐  
                                                                 │ 4\. MAC Comparison     │  
                                                                 │ calcMac \== storedMac? │  
                                                                 └───────────┬───────────┘  
                                                                             │  
                                            ┌────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┐  
                                            │ Match (Authentic)                                               │ Mismatch (Tampered)  
                                            ▼                                                                 ▼  
                            ┌────────────────────────────────┐                               ┌────────────────────────────────┐  
                            │ 5\. Safe to Decrypt & Serve     │                               │ 5\. HALT & REJECT               │  
                            │ Proceed with RSA/ECC decrypt   │                               │ Return HTTP 403 Forbidden      │  
                            │ in RAM; return to client       │                               │ "CRITICAL\_TAMPER\_ALERT"        │  
                            └────────────────────────────────┘                               └────────────────────────────────┘

#### Integrity Verification Protocol Table

| Step | Operation | Technical Mechanism | Security Purpose |
| :---: | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1** | Record Retrieval | MongoDB Driver / Mongoose | Retrieves target document (post, user, or order) containing ciphertexts and integrityMac. |
| **2** | Canonical Serialization | Deterministic String Builder | Concatenates critical ciphertext attributes and nonces in fixed order (e.g., titleEnc \+ contentEnc \+ authorId). |
| **3** | HMAC Computation | From-scratch hmac.ts | Feeds canonical string and server-side secret pepper into HMAC-SHA256 ($K' \oplus \text{ipad} \parallel \dots$). |
| **4** | Constant-Time Equality | Byte-by-byte comparison | Compares recomputed digest with stored integrityMac in constant time to prevent timing side-channel attacks. |
| **5a** | Authentic Match (✔) | Memory Decryption | Authenticity confirmed. System invokes RSA (decryptProfile) or ECC (decryptData) in RAM and serves plaintext. |
| **5b** | Tampered Mismatch (✘) | Emergency Abort | Halts execution immediately\! Throws 403 CRITICAL\_TAMPER\_ALERT, preventing attacker-controlled ciphertext manipulation. |

flowchart TD  
    Fetch\["1. Read Document & Stored integrityMac"\] \--\> Canon\["2. Build Canonical Payload from Encrypted Attributes"\]  
    Canon \--\> Calc\["3. Compute HMAC-SHA256 with Server Pepper Key"\]  
    Calc \--\> Test{"4. Does Computed MAC \== Stored MAC?"}  
    Test \-- Match (Authentic) \--\> Decrypt\["5a. Asymmetric Decryption in RAM & Return Data"\]  
    Test \-- Mismatch (Tampered) \--\> Halt\["5b. HALT\! Deny Decryption & Return HTTP 403 Alert"\]

If an attacker modifies ciphertext or changes document parameters directly in the database, the stored MAC will no longer match the recalculated MAC. The server immediately halts processing, denies decryption, and returns a 403 CRITICAL\_TAMPER\_ALERT.

## 10\. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) enforces strict privilege boundaries, preventing regular users from executing administrative tasks or accessing sensitive system controls.

---

### 10.1 Roles Defined

The system defines four distinct user roles:

1. **Admin (admin)**: Possesses complete oversight. Authorized to inspect all user accounts, view system audit logs, rotate cryptographic keys, manage the global menu catalog, and moderate community content.  
2. **Customer (customer)**: Regular user role. Authorized to update their personal profile, place orders, track deliveries, chat with assigned riders, and create or edit their own posts.  
3. **Restaurant Manager (restaurant)**: Operations role. Authorized to manage menu availability, track live orders in the kitchen pipeline, and assign riders for delivery.  
4. **Delivery Rider (rider)**: Logistics role. Authorized to view assigned deliveries, access delivery instructions, communicate with customers, and mark orders complete.

---

### 10.2 Permission Matrix

The table below outlines our role-permission structure:

| Operation / Resource | Admin | Customer (Regular User) | Restaurant | Delivery Rider |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **View own profile** | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |
| **Edit own profile** | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |
| **Create community posts** | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |
| **Edit own community posts** | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |
| **Delete ANY community post** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |
| **View all registered accounts** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |
| **Manage & rotate crypto keys** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |
| **Update menu catalog items** | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✘ |
| **Assign delivery riders** | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✘ |
| **Mark orders as delivered** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |
| **Access /admin/\* portal routes** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |

Every route is guarded by our Next.js edge middleware (src/middleware.ts), which checks token claims and redirects unauthorized users away from restricted pages.

---

## 11\. Secure Session Management

To defend against session hijacking, fixation, and replay attacks, authentication tokens and session identifiers are managed using strict security standards.

---

### 11.1 Token Signing and Verification

* **Stateless Signed JWTs**: BiteRush 2.0 uses NextAuth.js configured with a JSON Web Token (JWT) strategy. Tokens are cryptographically signed on the server with HMAC-SHA256 using NEXTAUTH\_SECRET.  
* **Session Hijacking Defenses**:  
  * **HttpOnly Cookies**: Session cookies are marked HttpOnly \= true, making them completely inaccessible to client-side JavaScript. This prevents session theft via Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).  
  * **SameSite Enforcement**: Cookies use SameSite \= Lax to defend against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).  
  * **Secure Flag**: In production environments, cookies use the Secure flag, restricting transmission exclusively to encrypted HTTPS connections.  
* **Per-Request Verification**: Every request intercepted by src/middleware.ts calls getToken({ req }). The middleware verifies the cryptographic signature, checks expiration timestamps, and validates role privileges before allowing access.

## 13\. Conclusion

The development of **BiteRush 2.0** demonstrates how full-stack web development can be paired with rigorous, low-level mathematical security. Rather than relying on framework abstractions, building **RSA-1024**, **ECC secp256k1 ElGamal**, **SHA-256**, **HMAC**, and **One-Time Passwords (OTP)** from scratch provided practical insight into applied number theory and defensive systems engineering.

Throughout implementation, key challenges included:

* Handling elliptic curve point additions and doubling without precision loss using native BigInt.  
* Deriving modular square roots on finite fields using the Tonelli-Shanks algorithm to embed plaintext messages into elliptic curve points.  
* Integrating a two-step OTP verification challenge into stateless NextAuth workflows.  
* Designing deterministic HMAC blind lookup tokens to allow fast database queries over encrypted emails and phone numbers without revealing plaintext values.

The resulting application satisfies every requirement of the CSE447 Lab Project. It delivers an engaging, intuitive user experience while maintaining robust database compromise resistance, strict data integrity verification, and role-based access control across all operations.
